summary: Cabin & Health is an offline decision-support prototype for health events in a spacecraft cabin, where there may be no physician on board and no immediate contact with Earth. When a crew member reports a symptom or an emergency, the app asks only the questions that matter, shows the most urgent step first, and then guides the user one action at a time. It also shows five simulated cabin readings (pressure, O2, CO2, humidity, temperature) and checks them against NASA-STD-3001 reference values. One of these is inspired oxygen pressure (PiO2), which the app calculates. Every decision comes from fixed local rules, with no AI and no network at runtime. Each rule carries a verbatim quote from its source, and automated tests check it. "Not sure" is never treated as "no", and a missing value is never treated as normal. The app turns five scattered research files into one traceable tool that works in Turkish and English. It is an experimental prototype, not a diagnosis tool, and is not medically approved.
details:
What it does

Cabin & Health (Kabin ve Sağlık) is an offline decision-support prototype for health events in a spacecraft cabin, where there may be no physician on board and no immediate contact with Earth. When a crew member reports a symptom or an emergency, it asks only the questions that matter, shows the most urgent step first, and then guides the user one action at a time. Next to this, it shows five cabin readings from a built-in simulator and flags readings outside documented reference ranges.

How it works

1. Cabin dashboard and simulator: cabin pressure, ppO2, ppCO2, humidity and temperature, each with status, reading time and trend, always labelled "Simulation data". Cabin pressure is checked against 34.5 < P ≤ 103 kPa (NASA-STD-3001 Vol. 2 Rev. F, V2 6006). Oxygen is evaluated as inspired oxygen pressure, PiO2 (V2 6003, Table 6.2-1). The one-hour CO2 average is checked against ≤ 3 mmHg (V2 6004), and temperature and humidity against comfort ranges (V2 6013). Stopped data is shown as "not updating", never as current. The simulator has five scenarios (pressure drop, CO2 rise, heat/humidity, sensor failure), a manual mode, ×1/×60 speed and recovery.

2. Guided problem report: (1) one emergency screen with four large options; any of them shows urgent steps immediately; (2) 27 symptoms in 8 groups, multi-select; (3) only the needed questions, with each shared question asked once; (4) a "Do now" card with one action at a time; (5) six manual personal measurements (pulse, SpO2, blood pressure, temperature, respiratory rate, blood glucose) that never delay the first action; (6) follow-up with editable answers, evaluation history and reminders.

3. Rules engine: fixed, local rules with no AI and no network at runtime.

Safety-oriented design

Urgent first. "Not sure" is never "no": it shows as "could not be excluded — check". A missing value is never zero or normal. Cabin values are labelled "within the defined range", not "safe", and a possible cabin–symptom link is labelled as not proving the cause. Different things stay separate. For example, in low blood sugar, "no improvement after 10 minutes" (G_NOIMP) is a separate escalation from whether oral food or drink is allowed (alertness and swallowing).

Benefits and intended impact

The crew's knowledge was spread over five research files: symptom action cards, a symptom-to-measurement map, symptom-to-cabin links, personal measurement thresholds and cabin reference values. We turned them into one consistent, traceable tool, so that under stress the user sees the next step, not a long document.

Traceability

Every rule in the code carries a verbatim quotation from its source, and an automated test checks that the quotation appears word for word. Source data records the file, sheet, row and a SHA-256 fingerprint. Choices no source supports (question order, the 5-second stale-data timeout, the 95% coverage threshold) are marked as team design decisions. Conflicts between sources were resolved openly. Two research files disagreed on 12 symptoms, so we gave them separate roles. An old glucose rule that required a personal plan was replaced by the newer rule and kept as "superseded". Proposed oxygen percentages were checked and rejected because they are not ppO2 limits in the NASA standard.

Tools

HTML, CSS and plain JavaScript with no libraries or CDN, a zero-dependency Node.js server that blocks network connections, Python to read the Excel research files without changing them, and Node.js tests. 19,863 automated assertions pass, mostly translation coverage; they are software checks, not medical cases. The interface works in Turkish and English, in light and dark mode, and at phone width.

Creativity

Urgent steps interrupt the flow instead of waiting at the end. Each report is linked to a snapshot of the cabin at that moment. Every piece of guidance can be traced to its source, and an independent research review was used to find and fix real errors (glucose escalation, pressure bound, simulator crash).

Limits and responsible use

Cabin data is simulated. Medical thresholds come mostly from ground-based first aid (AHA, NHS, NIDDK, Red Cross and others), not approved spaceflight protocols, and microgravity techniques such as CPR are not covered. Medical content and translations have not been reviewed by a specialist, and no usability study has been done. The app does not diagnose and does not replace mission medical protocols. Using some NASA limits does not claim compliance with the standard.

Use of AI in development

AI was used only during research and development, never at runtime. The application code, automated tests, documentation, English translation and simplified Turkish wording were written with Claude Code (Anthropic) under the team's direction; every design decision was made by the team. An AI-assisted research review was also used to check our rules against the original sources, and each change it led to was verified in the code and tests. The research files were prepared by the team.
